                                         PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                             §             PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                          §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                        §                     OF TEXAS


                  COMMENTS OF THE TEXAS ENERGY BUYERS ALLIANCE

                                         I.​   INTRODUCTION

        The Texas Energy Buyers Alliance (TEBA) represents the collective voice of more than

200 companies, representing more than $36 trillion in market capitalization and hundreds of

thousands of employees in Texas across a diversity of energy customers, including data centers,

retail businesses, petrochemical companies, technology companies and manufacturers. As some

of the state’s largest employers and energy customers, our members share a common purpose: to

protect the efficient, reliable, low-cost ERCOT market. Our organization is focused on helping to

shape Texas’ electricity market redesign in ways that propel Texas’ economy forward, lower

power bills for all energy customers, create jobs, spur innovation, strengthen the ERCOT grid,

and grow Texas’ energy leadership.

        Because TEBA’s membership represents such a unique cross-section of businesses in Texas, we

feel we are uniquely qualified to provide insight into this question. New large loads will result in a new

major round of investments in transmission and generation infrastructure that could lower costs for all

consumers if there are no barriers put in place for investments in low-cost resources. TEBA emphasizes

that the integration of new large loads must be approached with a balanced framework that both

safeguards reliability and encourages economic investment across the state of Texas. Transparent and

predictable interconnection processes are critical to ensure that Texas remains competitive in attracting

large load customers.

        TEBA recognizes the nuances of implementation of Senate Bill 6’s requirements and appreciates

the time and effort that Commission staff has dedicated toward setting these important rules.
                                     II.​   GENERAL COMMENTS

        Many trade associations, consumer groups, and data center developers — of which TEBA is all

three — have focused their attention on the level of financial security required under this proposal. TEBA

will therefore limit our commentary to three topics: the refundability of financial security deposits, how a

minimum transmission charge can interact with the financial security requirements, and the use of

Regional Planning Group plans as a blueprint for connecting load that has already been planned for.

        On the subject of non-refundability, TEBA opposes the imposition of non-refundable security

requirements as a matter of principle when it functions as an excessive fee on doing business, as is the

case in this proposal. Non-refundability is appropriate when a developer has elected to move forward with

inclusion in a transmission plan that incorporates their loads, and should be limited to protecting other

customers from paying for costs incurred by the utility on their behalf if the developer does not ultimately

move forward. This proposal, however, imposes non-refundability before any load studies occur and

before any transmission is confirmed to be available, or when it might materialize.

        Relatedly, the implications of non-refundability in the context of corporate or parental guarantees

are not clearly addressed. There is a lack of clarity around the process for exercising corporate guarantee

payments for projects that do not move forward in the process. Once the guarantor is required to make a

payment on the nonrefundable piece, it is unclear how this capital would be requested by the utility upon

cancellation. TEBA recommends including this option as a cost effective mechanism for creditworthy

companies to meet financial commitments with less capital outlay. TEBA recommends that the best

approach to this scenario is to directly invoice a developer who leverages a parental guarantee if their

project is cancelled.

        The cost of credit is a central concern when it comes to upfront non-refundability. When required

up-front, many development partners will have to draw upon investor capital, which comes with a high

expectation for a return on investment. Capital held as collateral cannot be deployed toward productive

investments, one example being generation capacity investment. Reducing or eliminating upfront
 non-refundable payments would open the door to a more workable alternative: the minimum transmission

charges that TEBA has consistently proposed.

        For any refundable capital that is held, TEBA believes such funds should be kept in an escrow

account rather than retained by the utility. Utilities are not banks and asking them to maintain these large

amounts of customer funds introduces risk unnecessarily. The funds should be released upon satisfaction

of specific agreed-upon conditions and promptly returned to the depositing party.

        While minimum transmission charges are not directly at issue in this rulemaking, TEBA strongly

encourages the Commission to consider the use of a minimum transmission charge — as proposed by

TEBA and multiple other stakeholders in Project No. 58484 — in connection with financial security

matters. Minimum transmission charges would be collected on an ongoing basis through retail bills as a

way to ensure new large loads pay for the transmission to serve them. To the extent that financial security

or interconnection deposits are held, the entire security deposit should be refundable upon the load

energizing and transitioning to minimum transmission charges. This would generate meaningful revenues

and if properly structured can protect other ratepayers from bearing unnecessary costs.

​       In addition, the most important opportunity in front of the Commission is to more closely align

the batch study process with work already completed through Regional Planning Groups, or “RPGs.”

RPG plans serve as ERCOT’s forward-looking framework for transmission development intended to meet

anticipated demand. They reflect load growth that utilities have identified and, in many cases, are already

planning infrastructure to serve. That is one of the clearest available indicators that a project is viable and

that the system is actively preparing to accommodate it. If a project is already embedded in an RPG plan,

that reflects system-level validation that should carry meaningful weight in how the initial batch is

structured. ERCOT uses any RPGs currently under independent review as a basis for supporting

additional load interconnections.

​       Finally, TEBA recommends extending the allowable delay window before capacity is reallocated,

as outlined in (h)(1), from 6 months to 12 months. A 6-month threshold is overly restrictive and fails to
 account for routine development delays outside a developer’s control, such as permitting timeslines,

supply chain constraints, and equipment lead times.

        Overall, these alternatives offer an effective substitute for several of the controversial policies

proposed in this rulemaking, and TEBA strongly encourages the Commission to consider adopting our

suggestions for the current nonrefundable security deposit and transmission planning provisions outlined

in this proposal for publication.
                                               V. CONCLUSION

        TEBA appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and looks forward to

continuing to work with Commission staff on this matter.



                                                           Respectfully submitted,

​                                                          /s/ Bryn Baker
​                                                          Bryn Baker
​                                                          Texas Energy Buyers Alliance
                                                           bbaker@txenergybuyers.com

RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                             §            PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                          §
STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                        §                    OF TEXAS


           EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF TEXAS ENERGY BUYERS ALLIANCE

 ●​ TEBA opposes imposing non-refundable security requirements before any load studies occur and

     before transmission is confirmed to be available, or when it might materialize.

 ●​ The implications of non-refundability in the context of corporate or parental guarantees are not

     clearly addressed. TEBA recommends that the best approach to this scenario is to directly invoice

     a developer who leverages a parental guarantee if their project is cancelled.

 ●​ For any refundable capital that is held, TEBA believes such funds should be kept in an escrow

     account rather than retained by the utility.

 ●​ TEBA strongly encourages the Commission to consider the use of a minimum transmission

     charge. The entire security deposit should be refundable upon the load energizing and

     transitioning to minimum transmission charges.

 ●​ It’s important that loads included in RPG plans are considered. If a project is already embedded in

     an RPG plan it should be included as base load in Batch Zero.

 ●​ TEBA recommends the allowable project delay window before capacity is reallocated be

     extended from 6 months to 12 months.
